That one came from Felix. Dependabot promised to automate away a chore many of us skipped because of the tedious, never-ending onslaught of updates, and when it launched, people loved it. Years later, I have a bad case of what I call dependency burnout. Dependabot bumps something, the build breaks, and now fixing it is my problem. Multiply that across every repo and I just stopped merging them altogether unless I needed a bugfix or a new feature. Meanwhile, the steady stream of new CVEs and zero-days has made keeping dependencies up to date more important than ever. And Dependabot hasnât really kept up. The alternatives donât always fare better in practice, either. At my $DAYJOB we use Renovate , but itâs been dialed way back. It only runs once a week and the rebase commands are turned off, so its PRs go stale and start conflicting before anyone gets to them. So I built Felix. The name is a nod to Fix-It Felix Jr. from Wreck-It Ralph , because the whole point is that it fixes things, and doesnât just bump numbers and walk away. ## Where todayâs update bots fall short Dependabot, Renovate, and the rest of the update bots are rigid in their approach. Find all the Cargo.toml , package.json , requirements.txt and lockfiles, check upstream for new versions, and if anything changed, update the manifest and lockfile and open a pull request. Thatâs kinda where it stops: - Upgrades are fragmented. If you use .tool-versions , mise.toml , Dockerfiles, and GitHub Actions, a toolchain upgrade lands in one place and the rest are left behind. - Major versions are your problem. Majors often need code changes. The bot opens the PR, CI goes red, and it sits there until you read the migration guide yourself. - No one reads the release notes. New APIs that would let you delete your workarounds go unnoticed. - Conflicts pile up. Merge one PR and the next three now conflict on the lockfile. Hope your rebase command isnât disabled. ## Where agents fit This is exactly the kind of work agents are great at. Itâs tedious, itâs well defined, and verifying it is just running the build and tests. Felix still does the boring deterministic parts the old way. Versions come from a registry lookup, never from the model, so it wonât invent a tag that doesnât exist. Then an agent takes over: it consults the release notes, makes the code changes, and looks for everything outside the dependency files that also needs to move. Moving FROM rust:1.99 also moves rust-toolchain.toml , the CI toolchain, .tool-versions , mise.toml , and anything else that names that Rust version. A coherence check gates every PR before it opens, so a half-finished upgrade never makes it to review. Thatâs why the Felix version of the Rust upgrade bumped both pins together. Felix also groups related changes instead of opening twelve PRs. Routine bumps get bundled, and anything risky, like a compiler major, gets its own PR. ### Automatic major version upgrades This is the part that motivated me to build Felix in the first place. It doesnât stop at minor and patch versions: it reads the upgrade guide, migrates config, fixes the code, and runs your build and tests in a sandbox on the new version before it opens anything. If the build broke and Felix had to fix it, the PR tells you what it changed and why. When I bumped Biome 1 â 2 , Felix migrated biome.json to the v2 schema and fixed the handful of new lint failures. It also called out which formatting diffs came from new v2 defaults, so I wasnât left guessing. Once Felix could handle an upgrade that big, I realized the same machinery works for changes that arenât upgrades at all. I call these campaigns: describe one change, and Felix rolls it out across all my repos, one PR each. So far Iâve used it on uuidgen.dev to add a justfile and to replace Next.js with TanStack Start . More on campaigns in a future post. ### Fixing its own PRs Felix watches CI on its own PRs. If a check fails, it tries to repair it. If merging one PR leaves another conflicting on the lockfile, Felix rebuilds that PR a few minutes later without asking. Lockfile-only conflicts skip the agent and just get regenerated. You can also talk to it. Comment /felix rebase on a PR, or use plain words like /felix split vitest out or /felix hold react at 19 , and the agent either does it or explains why it wonât. ### No setup required Felix is a GitHub App, so there is nothing to add to your CI and no config needed to get started. Once itâs installed, every repo gets scanned on a schedule. Repos that are archived, forked, or havenât seen a commit in a while get skipped. If you want to tune things, there is an optional .felix.toml for the schedule, a minimum release age, groups, and verify commands. ## Why not just use an agent? Fair question. I could open Claude Code in each repo, tell it to update the dependencies, and it would probably do a decent job. But âprobablyâ and âwhen I remember toâ are exactly the problems Iâm trying to get away from. The model is the smart part, but what makes Felix reliable is everything around it. - Itâs always on. A coding agent works when you ask it to. Felix is hosted, so it scans, watches CI, and rebuilds its PRs while Iâm off doing something else. Nobody has to remember to run it, which is the whole point when the problem is burnout. - Purpose-built tools, not just a shell. Instead of grepping around and guessing, the model gets tools built for this one job. lookup_versions asks the registries what actually exists. inspect_repo finds every pin of a toolchain or package and flags any that disagree. verify runs the build and tests and only reports errors that are new compared with the base branch. - Guardrails it canât talk its way around. open_pull_request refuses if the pins are out of sync, and opens a draft if any check failed. Every run has a budget, and an upgrade it gives up on is set aside instead of retried every night. - It remembers what you told it. Close a PR and Felix skips that version. Ignores, groups, and schedules live in .felix.toml , not in a prompt you retype every session. - Every PR reads the same. A table of changes, a âNeeds attentionâ section, and exactly what was verified. Reviewing them gets fast. ## Built on Cloudflare Naturally, the whole thing runs on Cloudflare. It never sees a GitHub credential: the Worker streams the repo in and commits through the GitHub API. - Models run on Workers AI . - D1 keeps track of runs and PRs, R2 holds the full build logs, and KV caches registry lookups. ### Agents with Flue The agent itself is built with Flue , an agent framework from the Astro team ( withastro/flue ). Rather than wiring up raw LLM API calls and a tool loop myself, Flue gives you the harness: the model, tools, a sandbox, and sub-agents, all declared in plain TypeScript. It also ships Cloudflare support out of the box, so the sandbox is a Container and the models come straight from the Workers AI binding. Here is roughly what Felixâs agent looks like, trimmed down: export function Updater () { useModel ( SMALL_MODEL ); useSandbox ( cloudflareSandbox ( /* this repo's container */ )); useTool (lookupVersions); useTool (releaseNotes); // ... useSubagent ({ name: 'pr_worker' , model: SMALL_MODEL /* ... */ }); useSubagent ({ name: 'pr_expert' , model: LARGE_MODEL /* ... */ }); return PROMPT ; } ### Two models, cheap by default Most dependency updates are boring, and they donât need a big model. Felix uses two: - DeepSeek V4.1 Flash does almost everything. It plans the run, splits the work into PRs, and hands each PR to a pr_worker sub-agent that edits, builds, verifies, and opens it. - GLM-5.3 is the expert. The planner only calls pr_expert when a worker is stuck, a CI repair has already failed once, or a major clearly needs real code changes. Each PR gets a fresh sub-agent that reports back only a few lines, so build logs never pile up in the plannerâs context. That keeps runs cheaper and more reliable. A deterministic pre-scan means the model only runs on repos with something to update. Every run has a hard budget, $1.50 by default. ## Some of my favorite PRs - Biome 1 â 2 : the one from above.
